title: Renewal check-in: usage + spend forecast (Fabrikam)
summary: Fabrikam walked through their March–May spend forecast for Redwood Hosted API and highlighted two pain points: (1) day-to-day volatility (model mix changes, retries/fallback, and caching behavior) and (2) internal budgeting requirements that prefer commit + predictable overages. Redwood shared recent metering hardening work (idempotency/dedupe on retries, billed vs raw tokens, cache-hit attribution fields, and a short shadow-billing compare period) and clarified what will and will not change in invoicing. The group discussed packaging options: staying pure PAYG with better alerting and daily exports, moving to an annual commit with discounted overage, or adding Dedicated capacity for the steady baseline and bursting to Hosted for peaks. Redwood agreed to send a proposal with two options (Hosted commit-only vs hybrid Dedicated+Hosted), plus updated guidance explaining billed tokens, cache hits, and retry accounting for procurement and finance review.
topics: Spend forecast review (last 60 days, next 90 days)
Drivers of volatility: retries/fallback, streaming, caching, model mix
Meter definitions: billed tokens vs raw tokens; cache-hit attribution; idempotency
Packaging options: commit + overage; Dedicated baseline + Hosted burst
Procurement requirements: predictability, dispute language, usage export format/timezone
Next steps for renewal proposal + technical validation
questions: Can we cap monthly spend or hard-fail requests once a budget is hit?
If your servers retry/fallback, are we billed twice?
How do you count tokens for streaming responses and tool calls?
If cache hits reduce compute, do we see that reflected in billed usage and exports?
Can invoices and usage exports be aligned to our finance timezone (PT) and month-end close cutoff?
action_items: Jordan Blake: Send renewal proposal with two options (Hosted commit-only vs hybrid Dedicated+Hosted) including overage rates and SLA assumptions by 2026-02-28
Rishi Malhotra: Provide a one-page forecast model template (inputs: tokens by model, cache-hit %, retry rate) for Fabrikam FinOps to run scenarios by 2026-03-01
Soojin Lee: Share customer-facing wording draft for billed vs raw tokens + caching + retries (procurement-friendly) by 2026-03-01
Samir Khan: Export a sample week of request logs with request_id/idempotency_key + model + region + cache flags so Redwood can sanity-check volatility drivers by 2026-03-04
Mark Weber: Confirm Fabrikam’s preferred invoice/usage export timezone and month-end usage freeze expectations by 2026-03-04
next_steps: Redwood to deliver pricing proposal and packaging recommendation for renewal/expansion.
Schedule a 30-min technical session to review billed token fields, cache-hit attribution, and retry/fallback behavior with Fabrikam ML platform.
Procurement to review usage definition/dispute language once Redwood shares the updated wording.
Revisit whether a Dedicated baseline makes sense after Redwood provides GPU-seconds estimate for steady traffic.
transcript:
Meeting: Renewal check-in: usage + spend forecast (Fabrikam)
Recorded: 2026-02-25 17:00 UTC
Duration: 46 min
Attendees:
- Jordan Blake (Redwood) 
- Rishi Malhotra (Redwood) 
- Soojin Lee (Redwood)
- Priya Desai (Fabrikam)
- Mark Weber (Fabrikam)
- Elena Ruiz (Fabrikam)
- Samir Khan (Fabrikam)

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
- Fabrikam is forecasting higher usage next quarter driven by new in-product copilots.
- Fabrikam wants tighter spend predictability; asks about commits, overages, and whether retries are double-billed.
- Redwood reviewed metering updates: stronger idempotency, billed_tokens field, cache-hit attribution, and shadow billing compares.
- Next steps: Redwood to send two packaging options and a one-page metering/usage definition for procurement.


[00:00] Jordan Blake: Alright, I think we’re good. Priya, Mark, Elena, Samir — thanks for making time. The goal today is pretty straightforward: you all have a renewal coming up, and you’d asked for a spend forecast review and options that make budgeting less painful.

[00:14] Priya Desai: Yep. Thanks Jordan. We’ve got Finance breathing down our neck a little bit, so we want to get ahead of it.

[00:20] Mark Weber: And also, we had a couple of weird spikes in January that made our forecast look, uh, kind of embarrassing.

[00:28] Jordan Blake: Yeah, totally. We pulled the last 60-ish days usage and I think we’re aligned on where those spikes came from, but let’s go through it with you. Rishi’s on to help with the spend model, and Soojin can speak to packaging and what we can put in writing for procurement.

[00:43] Elena Ruiz: Hi. Just flagging, for renewal we’ll need very crisp definitions of “usage” and the dispute window language. The last redline round got stuck on token counting.

[00:54] Soojin Lee: Yep, heard. We’ve been tightening that up, especially around retries and caching. We can share a procurement-friendly version.

[01:03] Samir Khan: And I’m mostly here because I got pulled in after the “double billed tokens” thread. I want to understand what you count and where it shows up.

[01:12] Jordan Blake: Great. Mark, do you want to start with what you’re forecasting?

[01:16] Mark Weber: Sure. Let me try to summarize. So, baseline today is about—call it 120 to 140 million tokens a day across two models. Then we have a March release that bumps that maybe 30%. April might double if the sales team rolls it out to the rest of the SKUs.

[01:35] Rishi Malhotra: When you say tokens, is that prompt plus completion, or just completion?

[01:39] Mark Weber: That’s total as reported in your usage export. Which I think is prompt and completion. But this is part of the problem: our internal metric is “requests” and “characters,” not tokens.

[01:51] Rishi Malhotra: Got it. And just to align terms, the export you’re looking at right now — that’s “billed tokens” or the older “raw tokens” view?

[01:58] Mark Weber: Uh. I think it just says tokens.

[02:01] Samir Khan: It’s the endpoint where we pull daily totals by model and day. It’s… I can find the name later.

[02:07] Jordan Blake: That’s okay. We can address that because we’ve added fields recently that separate raw vs billed, and also cache hit attribution. But let’s stay on your goals: predictability, and eliminating surprises.

[02:20] Priya Desai: Exactly. We’re not trying to nickel and dime. But we need to be able to say, “This feature costs X,” and not have it swing 25% because of like, retries or whatever.

[02:34] Jordan Blake: Makes sense. So let’s talk about the January spikes. Our view was: two drivers. One, a model mix shift — you moved more traffic to the larger model for about five days.

[02:46] Mark Weber: That’s true.

[02:47] Jordan Blake: And two, there was an elevated retry rate on streaming calls when you had client timeouts. Samir, I think you were using a 10 second timeout at the gateway?

[02:56] Samir Khan: That sounds right. We changed it later.

[02:59] Jordan Blake: So the key question you asked us is, “Are we billed twice when there’s a retry or fallback.” Historically, the industry has been a mess there, and we’ve been hardening our own metering to make it consistent.

[03:13] Elena Ruiz: I’m going to interrupt: we need an answer that we can put in the contract. Not “it depends.”

[03:18] Jordan Blake: Yep. The contract answer is: you pay for successful usage as defined, and we do not intentionally double-charge server-side retries for the same request. Practically, the implementation depends on idempotency. Rishi, do you want to explain it in plain English?

[03:33] Rishi Malhotra: Sure. We’re moving toward a model where each request has a stable request identifier — either what you pass (idempotency_key) or what we generate — and then usage events dedupe on that. If we have to retry internally, it should map back to the same “billable event.”

[03:50] Samir Khan: “Should.” That’s what I don’t like.

[03:53] Rishi Malhotra: Fair. We found some edge cases specifically on streaming where partial chunks plus retry could emit two usage events. Engineering has a fix in rollout, and we’ve been running “shadow billing compare” where we compute old and new meters in parallel before it affects invoices.

[04:12] Priya Desai: Does that mean our invoice might change next month?

[04:14] Jordan Blake: No retroactive changes without approval and notice. Any meter fixes that change numbers — the default is forward-looking. If we ever needed to credit because you were overbilled, we’d handle it as a credit, not silently rewrite history.

[04:28] Elena Ruiz: Good. Put that in writing.

[04:30] Soojin Lee: We can. Also, we can define the dispute window and how we handle late-arriving usage events, which was another concern.

[04:38] Mark Weber: Late arriving events is huge. Our month-end close is tight. We can’t have usage from the 31st showing up on the 3rd.

[04:46] Jordan Blake: Understood. We can align on a “usage freeze” cutoff for invoicing. You’ll still see events trickle into the raw telemetry sometimes, but the invoiced ledger will use the freeze window. That’s something Finance and Legal set, but we can propose a standard.

[05:04] Priya Desai: Okay. Back to forecast. Our main ask is: what options do we have so we can tell Finance, “Here’s the committed spend, here’s overage if we exceed.”

[05:16] Jordan Blake: Perfect. There are basically three packaging paths:
1) Stay on pure usage-based Hosted API, but improve predictability with budget alerts, daily exports in your timezone, and maybe a soft cap.
2) Hosted commit: you commit to an annual dollar amount or token bundle, get a better rate, and overage is a defined price per million tokens.
3) Hybrid: Dedicated capacity for your steady baseline throughput, and burst to Hosted for spikes. Dedicated is metered in GPU-seconds, but contracted as a monthly commit.

[05:46] Mark Weber: Option two is what Finance wants. Option three is what Engineering wants.

[05:52] Samir Khan: Yeah, I’d prefer dedicated for baseline. We can control latency better and not be surprised by noisy neighbors.

[05:58] Priya Desai: But dedicated sounds like we’re paying even when we’re idle.

[06:02] Jordan Blake: That’s the trade. Dedicated improves consistency and can be cheaper at high utilization, but you’re reserving capacity.

[06:10] Rishi Malhotra: For forecasting, we usually model it as: baseline tokens/day at an expected tokens-per-GPU-second efficiency, then compute required GPU-seconds. You can also do a smaller dedicated pool and let autoscale handle some variability.

[06:25] Mark Weber: I need numbers. Like, real numbers.

[06:28] Jordan Blake: Yep. We’ll send a proposal with two options. One is a Hosted commit-only. The other is a hybrid with a smaller Dedicated baseline.

[06:38] Elena Ruiz: And the overage terms need to be explicit. No “we’ll invoice at list price.”

[06:44] Soojin Lee: Agreed. We can include a rate card with included usage and overage rate, plus how credits apply.

[06:52] Mark Weber: Speaking of credits: we had confusion on when credits apply. Like do they apply to the most expensive model first or…?

[06:59] Jordan Blake: Good question. Our default is credits apply to eligible usage on your invoice, typically oldest credits first, across the eligible product line. But we can clarify eligibility and ordering in the order form.

[07:12] Samir Khan: Can you clarify caching? Because we’re experimenting with prompt caching on our side and also your side. I saw something about “cache hit.”

[07:20] Jordan Blake: Yeah. So there are two concepts:
- If you cache on your side and don’t call us, you obviously don’t pay.
- If Redwood serves a response using prefix/KV cache within our runtime, it still involves serving, but less compute. We now expose a cache_hit signal and separate “raw tokens” from “billed tokens” so you can see what got discounted or attributed.

[07:44] Priya Desai: Wait, does cache hit mean we pay less?

[07:47] Jordan Blake: Depending on plan and endpoint, yes, that’s the direction. But I don’t want to overpromise without the exact plan language. Soojin can send the current policy and what’s in pilot.

[07:58] Soojin Lee: Right. For some packages we treat cache hits as billed tokens but at a discounted rate, or we track them separately for reporting. The main point is transparency: you’ll see billed_tokens and cache_hit_tokens in exports.

[08:13] Mark Weber: That would help. Today it’s kind of a black box. We only see total tokens and then a big number.

[08:20] Rishi Malhotra: For volatility, the biggest drivers we usually see are:
- completion length drift (prompting changes)
- model routing changes (bigger model, more tokens)
- retries/timeouts (client side) and fallback (server side)
- cache hit rate moving around
So we can build a scenario model with those as inputs.

[08:41] Samir Khan: On retries: if our client times out and retries with a new idempotency key, that’s on us, right?

[08:49] Jordan Blake: Correct. If you send a truly new request, we can’t infer it’s the same. If you send the same idempotency key, we’ll dedupe. That’s why we recommend you use idempotency keys on any request that could be retried by your infra.

[09:04] Samir Khan: We do for non-streaming. For streaming, it’s trickier.

[09:08] Jordan Blake: Totally. That’s one of the places we’re investing: consistent behavior for streaming reconnects, partial responses, and tool calls.

[09:18] Priya Desai: Okay, can we talk about what we can put in a renewal doc that addresses Mark’s predictability needs?

[09:26] Jordan Blake: Yep. Proposed structure:
- An annual commit amount (or quarterly) that covers expected baseline usage at a discounted rate.
- A defined overage price per million tokens.
- Optional: a spend notification threshold and a “soft cap” where we alert and require an admin to raise limits.
- A usage definition addendum: billed tokens, handling of retries/fallback, streaming semantics.

[09:55] Elena Ruiz: And dispute process.

[09:56] Jordan Blake: And dispute process — yes.

[10:00] Mark Weber: Also exports. Our BI pipeline expects a daily CSV at 00:00 PT. Right now it’s like UTC and we have to shift it.

[10:09] Jordan Blake: We can align exports to PT. We’ve had other customers ask. There might be some nuance around when the day “closes,” but we can do it.

[10:21] Rishi Malhotra: And to Elena’s point, we should also specify whether the invoice is based on the usage API exports or the billing ledger. The ledger is the source of truth, but we can guarantee reconciliation between them within a tolerance.

[10:34] Elena Ruiz: That’s exactly what we need. Because last year, we had “invoice differs from usage API” and it turned into a whole thing.

[10:41] Jordan Blake: Understood. We’ve actually been building internal drift checks so those mismatches get caught before invoices go out.

[10:49] Samir Khan: Is that because you had metering bugs?

[10:51] Jordan Blake: We’ve had the typical issues you see in any telemetry pipeline: missing dimensions, late events, edge cases on retries. That’s why we’re tightening it now. But again, no surprises: we’ll communicate changes and we’re running shadow comparisons.

[11:08] Priya Desai: Let’s get back to the forecast numbers, because I have a meeting after this.

[11:13] Jordan Blake: Yep. Rishi, can you walk through what you computed from their last 60 days?

[11:19] Rishi Malhotra: Sure. Based on your usage export:
- Average daily billed tokens: ~132M
- 95th percentile day: ~178M (this includes the January spike window)
- Model A: ~70% of tokens, Model B: ~30% but drives ~55% of spend due to rate
We also saw completion lengths trending up about 12% month-over-month, likely from prompt changes.

[11:46] Mark Weber: That tracks.

[11:48] Rishi Malhotra: For March–May, if we assume the 30% increase Priya mentioned, you’re at ~170M/day average. If April doubles, you’re closer to ~260M/day average.

[12:05] Mark Weber: That’s the scary number.

[12:07] Priya Desai: It won’t double forever. It’s more like a rollout wave.

[12:10] Rishi Malhotra: Exactly. So what we can propose is a commit that covers, say, 180M/day equivalent usage, with defined overage for the wave months.

[12:23] Elena Ruiz: A commit is fine as long as unused doesn’t just vanish monthly. We prefer annual true-up.

[12:29] Jordan Blake: We can do annual commit with monthly invoicing, and carry-forward within the term. We’ll put specifics in the proposal.

[12:39] Samir Khan: If we go dedicated baseline, how do we measure it? I’ve heard “GPU hours,” “GPU seconds,” and it’s always confusing.

[12:47] Jordan Blake: Dedicated is tracked as GPU-seconds consumed by your pool. The contract would usually be a reserved capacity commit — like X GPUs for Y hours — but internally we reconcile to GPU-seconds for transparency. There are details around idle time and autoscaling transitions.

[13:07] Samir Khan: Idle time is what I’m worried about. If we provision 8 GPUs and only use 4 half the day, are we paying for 8 all day?

[13:16] Jordan Blake: Under a strict reservation, yes. Under an autoscaling policy, it can scale down, but then you trade for warm-up time. Again, it’s a baseline vs burst discussion.

[13:28] Priya Desai: For now, assume we stick with hosted, but I want the option to add dedicated later. Can we structure that?

[13:35] Jordan Blake: Yes. We can do a hosted commit now and include an addendum that lets you convert some portion of commit into Dedicated if you decide in Q2.

[13:47] Elena Ruiz: That’s helpful.

[13:49] Mark Weber: Okay, but if you’re changing meters, how does that impact our forecast? Like, if billed tokens changes definition, my forecast is wrong.

[13:59] Rishi Malhotra: Great point. We are not changing the core tokenization for your endpoints in a way that would swing numbers materially. The fixes we’re doing are mostly correctness: removing duplicates on retries, aligning streaming accounting, and adding dimensions. In most cases, it should reduce surprise variance, not create it.

[14:18] Samir Khan: But if you remove duplicates, our billed usage might go down.

[14:21] Jordan Blake: Potentially, yes, for cases where you were effectively being double-counted. But we’re not going to apply it retroactively unless there’s a clear overbill and we decide to credit.

[14:31] Priya Desai: That’s fine. If it goes down later, I’ll take the win.

[14:35] Mark Weber: Finance will take the win too.

[14:37] Jordan Blake: Exactly.

[14:39] Elena Ruiz: One more legal point: if a request fails mid-stream, what happens? Are we billed for partial tokens?

[14:46] Jordan Blake: It depends on the failure mode. If we delivered tokens to you, those are real compute and typically billable; if it fails before any output is delivered, it should not be billed. We can define this in the usage terms — like “tokens successfully generated and transmitted.”

[15:05] Samir Khan: That’s… contentious.

[15:07] Elena Ruiz: It’s exactly contentious.

[15:09] Soojin Lee: We can craft language that’s consistent and defensible. We usually define it around “output tokens delivered” and also ensure the usage export reflects what was delivered. Plus, we have the request_id so disputes can be investigated.

[15:25] Mark Weber: I don’t want to dispute every month. I want to never have to dispute.

[15:29] Jordan Blake: Same. That’s why we’re investing in drift checks and clear exports.

[15:36] Priya Desai: Alright, can we talk about discounting? We’ve been good customers. We’re growing. We want a rate that reflects that.

[15:44] Jordan Blake: Yes. The two levers are: commit size and term length. If you can do an annual commit that covers your baseline, we can improve the rate. Overages would still be defined, but typically slightly higher than the committed rate.

[15:59] Mark Weber: As long as overage isn’t punitive.

[16:02] Jordan Blake: It won’t be punitive. The goal is predictability and to avoid “gotcha” bills.

[16:07] Samir Khan: Are you going to ask us to change how we send requests? Like idempotency keys everywhere?

[16:12] Jordan Blake: We’ll recommend it. It’s not mandatory, but it’s best practice. Monica on our SDK team has been aligning defaults so it’s easier.

[16:23] Priya Desai: Samir, we should do that anyway.

[16:25] Samir Khan: Yeah. I just want to understand what “dedupe window” is. If I retry 5 minutes later, is it deduped?

[16:32] Jordan Blake: Typically dedupe is within a window tied to the idempotency key and request hash. We can share the exact behavior. The goal is that legitimate retried requests with the same key do not create extra usage.

[16:49] Mark Weber: Can you send that detail? Even if it’s in a doc.

[16:52] Soojin Lee: Yes. We’ll send a short technical note.

[16:57] Priya Desai: I’m going to ask the annoying question: Can we just have a fixed monthly bill?

[17:03] Jordan Blake: You can get close with a commit. A truly fixed bill ignores your growth and usage spikes. But we can structure it as: base commit billed monthly, with overage. That’s what most teams do.

[17:17] Elena Ruiz: Procurement will still ask for a cap.

[17:20] Jordan Blake: We can add optional controls — like hard limit, or “require approval to raise limit.” But it can impact availability if you hit it.

[17:31] Priya Desai: That’s okay. We’d rather fail closed than blow budget.

[17:36] Samir Khan: I’d rather degrade gracefully, not fail.

[17:39] Jordan Blake: There are options: you can implement fallback to a cheaper model when you approach budget, or throttle. We can help design that.

[17:50] Rishi Malhotra: From a forecast standpoint, one thing that helps is tracking cost per successful request. If you can share request counts and average tokens per request, we can translate to spend with less noise.

[18:02] Mark Weber: We have request counts. Tokens per request has been trending up, which we’re trying to rein in.

[18:08] Priya Desai: That’s product. They keep adding more context.

[18:11] Jordan Blake: That’s common. We can also talk about optimization, like caching and prompt compression, but maybe not today.

[18:20] Samir Khan: Quick question: tool calls. We’re using function calling for our ticket triage. Does that add tokens? Are those billed?

[18:28] Jordan Blake: Yes, tool call inputs/outputs are part of the model context, so they’re tokens. In the export you’ll see the total. We’re also making attribution clearer so it’s not mysterious.

[18:41] Priya Desai: Okay.

[18:43] Elena Ruiz: And what about reranking and embeddings? Are they separate meters?

[18:47] Jordan Blake: Yes. Embeddings are priced per input unit; chat/generation is tokens; rerank is per query/document pair. For renewal, we can keep them on the same order form but distinct line items.

[19:02] Mark Weber: Our spend is 90% generation, so focus there.

[19:06] Jordan Blake: Makes sense.

[19:08] Priya Desai: Can you share what a “good” cache hit rate looks like and how much it impacts bill?

[19:13] Jordan Blake: We can give guidance, but it depends on your traffic shape. If you have repeated prefixes, caching can help a lot. The important part is you’ll be able to see cache_hit attribution in the usage API so you can correlate.

[19:28] Samir Khan: We don’t see that today.

[19:30] Jordan Blake: You will soon, if not already. It’s rolling out across accounts.

[19:36] Mark Weber: I’ll believe it when I can query it.

[19:38] Jordan Blake: Fair.

[19:40] Soojin Lee: We can also provide a sample export schema. Like, columns: date, model, region, billed_tokens_prompt, billed_tokens_completion, raw_tokens, cache_hit_tokens, request_count, etc.

[19:56] Elena Ruiz: Region is important for us because we have data residency requirements. We need to know if usage is in US or EU.

[20:03] Jordan Blake: Yes, and that’s also important for pricing because regions can have different cost profiles. We’ve been fixing region dimension consistency.

[20:13] Priya Desai: We’re US-only right now.

[20:15] Elena Ruiz: But we might expand to EU. So include it.

[20:20] Jordan Blake: Will do.

[20:22] Mark Weber: Okay. So what do you need from us to finalize a proposal?

[20:26] Jordan Blake: Three things:
1) Confirm your forecast ranges: baseline, likely, high case.
2) Confirm your preference: annual commit with carry-forward, and acceptable overage.
3) Any non-negotiables: cap controls, export timezone, dispute window.

[20:47] Priya Desai: Baseline: 170M tokens/day. High case: 260M for April, then back down.

[20:54] Mark Weber: For Finance, we want an annual commit that covers baseline. Overages for April we can stomach, but not at list.

[21:04] Elena Ruiz: Non-negotiables: clear usage definition, no double billing on retries, dispute window of at least 30 days, and export/invoice alignment. Also confidentiality for pricing.

[21:16] Jordan Blake: Understood.

[21:18] Samir Khan: For engineering: if we do commit-only hosted, can we still get priority capacity? Like we had one incident where latency spiked.

[21:27] Jordan Blake: We can add a premium SLA tier or dedicated capacity. Hosted commit doesn’t automatically mean reserved GPUs, but we can include throughput guarantees depending on plan. That’s something we’ll propose.

[21:42] Priya Desai: We’re open to a small dedicated pool if it’s not crazy.

[21:46] Jordan Blake: That’s the hybrid option. We’ll size it based on your steady QPS.

[21:52] Rishi Malhotra: Samir, can you share a representative week of QPS and token distributions? Mean and p95. That helps estimate dedicated sizing.

[22:01] Samir Khan: Yes. I can export logs. We have request_id, model, tokens, and latency.

[22:08] Jordan Blake: Perfect.

[22:10] Mark Weber: One more thing. Those January spikes — can you guarantee that won’t happen again due to your own retries?

[22:18] Jordan Blake: We can’t guarantee there will never be retries in distributed systems, but we can guarantee we will not bill duplicates for the same idempotent request under the defined policy. And we can provide transparency: request-level tracing and usage records.

[22:35] Elena Ruiz: Put it in the language.

[22:36] Soojin Lee: Yep.

[22:38] Priya Desai: Are you changing tokenization? Like, are you switching token counter libraries?

[22:44] Jordan Blake: Not in a way that changes your counts unexpectedly. We align token counting across endpoints, including OpenAI-compatible ones, to reduce confusion. If there’s any change, we’d announce and run shadow comparisons.

[22:59] Samir Khan: We use your OpenAI-compatible endpoint for a couple services. That’s where we saw mismatch before.

[23:06] Jordan Blake: Right. That’s been a known issue industry-wide; we’ve been aligning those semantics.

[23:12] Mark Weber: Okay.

[23:14] Priya Desai: I think we’re good. Can we just confirm next steps so we’re not chasing you?

[23:20] Jordan Blake: Yep. Here’s what I captured:
- We’ll send a proposal with two options by end of week: Hosted commit-only and hybrid Dedicated+Hosted.
- Rishi will send a one-page forecast model template for you to plug in assumptions (model mix, cache hit, retry rate).
- Soojin will send procurement-friendly usage definition language: billed vs raw tokens, caching, retries, streaming partials, dispute window.
- Samir will send a sample week of logs so we can validate the volatility drivers and size dedicated if you want it.
- Mark/Elena will confirm timezone (PT) and the month-end freeze expectations.

[23:55] Mark Weber: Yes.

[23:56] Elena Ruiz: Yes.

[23:57] Samir Khan: Yes.

[23:58] Priya Desai: Works.

[24:00] Jordan Blake: Great. Any last questions?

[24:03] Mark Weber: Just one. If we increase commit later mid-term, do we get the better rate retroactively?

[24:09] Jordan Blake: Typically we adjust going forward. Sometimes we can true-up if it’s a bigger expansion, but we’ll specify it in the order form.

[24:19] Elena Ruiz: Okay.

[24:20] Samir Khan: And if we do dedicated later, can we convert commit?

[24:24] Jordan Blake: We can propose a conversion mechanism, yes.

[24:28] Priya Desai: Cool.

[24:30] Jordan Blake: Alright. Thanks everyone. We’ll follow up via email with the docs and schedule the technical session.

[24:38] (crosstalk)

[24:40] Elena Ruiz: Thanks.

[24:41] Mark Weber: Thanks.

[24:42] Priya Desai: Thanks.

[24:43] Samir Khan: Bye.

[End]

Notes (auto-detected)
- Competitors mentioned: Bedrock, OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Together
- Sentiment: Mostly neutral; budget predictability concerns; procurement wants clarity on usage definitions
- Risk flags: Meter definition confusion; invoice/export reconciliation expectations; month-end close cutoff
